title: Let go first (2:3)
hookLine: confessing without resolving is like immersing while still holding something impure
tomorrow: can a person actually become someone else?

cards: A message lands: so sorry about last night. Then, two bubbles later: but honestly you kind of started it. Sorry, but.
It shows up in texts, at work, across the dinner table. Can you say sorry while still holding on to it? Maimonides answers with a strange picture.
A person goes down into a mikveh, the pool of living water for ritual purity, and immerses, fully under. And in their fist, the whole time, is a sheretz, a dead creeping creature.

teach.b: Why that creature? In the Torah's purity laws, touching one makes a person impure. Leviticus says of the creeping things, "whosoever doth touch them, when they be dead, shall be unclean until the even."

teach.h: THE WATER CAN'T WASH WHAT YOU HOLD.
teach.b: So the water is working on the outside while the source of the problem stays in the hand. That's the puzzle solved: the immersion isn't weak. It's just being asked to wash something you won't put down.
Maimonides draws the line plainly. Someone who confesses in words but hasn't decided in their heart to leave the wrong is like that person in the pool.
The immersion doesn't help until the creature is thrown away. Then he gives a verse with two verbs: "whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy." Confessing alone is half the sentence.
The picture is older than Maimonides. The Talmud uses it too, and adds that such a person could immerse in all the waters of the world and still not be clean.
One more detail from the same passage: the confession should name the thing. Maimonides points to Moses, who doesn't say mistakes were made.
He says, "Oh, this people have sinned a great sin, and have made them gods of gold." Specific. So the order holds: open the hand, then the water works.

how: Immersion in a mikveh is part of Jewish purity practice and of conversion; the image of immersing while holding a sheretz is how the Talmud and Maimonides describe confession without change.

o: drop the wrong before you confess it
forgive the other person before they ask
release your feelings before you speak

games.q: the picture and its parts — tap the pairs.

s: if the confession is heartfelt enough, it works even if you keep doing it
Maimonides: confessing without deciding to leave is immersing with the sheretz still in hand.
the Talmud uses the sheretz picture too, before Maimonides
it says such a person could immerse in all the waters of the world and stay impure.
a confession should stay vague, so it stays dignified
Maimonides points to Moses naming it: a great sin, gods of gold.

games.q: a coworker says 'sorry I took credit for your slides' in a meeting, then leaves your name off the next deck too. what does the sheretz picture say about that sorry?
o: it isn't finished: the words came, but the credit-taking is still in hand.
it counts fully, because the apology was said in front of everyone.
it was too specific; a general sorry would have covered more ground.
games.why: words without leaving are immersion with the creature still in the fist. the verse needs both: confess and forsake.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees and close them into loose fists. Bring to mind one 'but' you've been holding, a grievance tucked inside an apology.
On a long breath out, open both hands, palms up, and leave them open for the rest of the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Let go first: Maimonides' rule that confession without leaving is like immersing with a sheretz in your hand. Open the hand, then the words.

orig.note: Hebrew: immersing with a sheretz in his hand, the Talmud's picture of confession without change.

carryVoice: For the road: let go first, because a sorry with a fist in it isn't finished yet. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Teshuvah 2:3 (confession without resolve; immersing with a sheretz; naming the sin)
Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 16a (one who confesses and does not turn back is like one holding a sheretz, even in all the waters of the world)
